nodes.title: Contact
nodes.body:
Everything here is made by hand by one person, so the person answering this email is the person who made your moisturiser. That has an obvious drawback, which is that I am sometimes in the workshop rather than at the desk. It also means nobody is going to read you a script.

Email store@biotaderm.com
Phone 01288 272800

I answer emails within one working day, usually the same day. The phone is better for anything urgent, though if it rings out it is because both hands are in a batch.

What to include

If it is about an order, the order number saves us a round trip. If it is about your skin, tell me what it is doing and what you have tried, and I will give you a straight answer even when the straight answer is that we do not make the thing you need.

Returns and the Two-Week Trial

If a product has not suited you, email and say so. You do not need to explain yourself, and you do not need to send a full bottle back. Everything you are entitled to is set out in our returns policy, including the 60-day trial and the 14-day statutory right to cancel.

Privacy

Anything you send goes to me and nowhere else. What happens to it is in our privacy policy.

Welcombe Skincare Ltd, trading as Biotaderm
Darracott Farm, Welcombe, Devon EX39 6HG, United Kingdom
Registered in England and Wales, company number 13451607

nodes.title: About Us
nodes.body:
Or, what happens when a chemist can't quite leave a question alone.

I'm Richard Bence, and I make Biotaderm. All of it, as it happens. I formulate the products, mix the batches, fill the bottles and answer the emails. It's a small operation on the north Devon coast, in Welcombe, and it began the way a lot of things do, with a problem I couldn't stop turning over.

nodes.title: Our Science
nodes.body:
How we think about skin, and how we show our working.

Skincare is full of confident promises and short on published evidence. This part of the site is where we slow down and set out the thinking behind the products: what we believe about skin, what actually goes into the bottle, and how we decide what we are willing to claim. Everything here links down to the detail, and the detail links to its sources.

Skin is a living system

Your skin is not a surface to be fixed. It is a living system, home to a microbiome of bacteria and other microbes that helps keep the barrier working and the whole thing in balance. Most of the time it knows what it is doing.

So we build products to support that system rather than override it. Support, not control. It is the quiet answer to a category full of quick fixes that promise to change your skin by Friday. We would rather work with your skin than against it, and we would rather show you why than ask you to take it on faith.

Formed in nature, led by science, guided by ethics

Three ideas run through everything, from the oils we press to the packaging we choose. They are intertwined, and they are easier to keep honest when they are written down.

Nature

The base of every product is cold-pressed organic plant oils, chosen for the bioactive compounds they carry rather than their price, the carotenoids, tocopherols, phytosterols and phenolics that refining tends to strip away. We leave out synthetic fragrance entirely, and never hide anything behind a "parfum" catch-all. The range does use a single essential oil, vetiver, and that is a deliberate choice we are happy to explain rather than bury. One ingredient also ties the range to where it is made: bladderwrack, the same Atlantic seaweed that grows on the rocks along the Devon coast, produced for us by specialist extractors in France. Kinship, not a supply chain.

How we formulate

Science

We think about skin the way current research does, as an ecosystem worth supporting. Prebiotics feed the microbes already living on your skin. Postbiotics are the useful compounds those microbes produce. Together they nudge things toward balance rather than stripping everything back and starting again. The discipline that matters most sits underneath all of it: Biotaderm reads the published science, it does not run it. So we credit the research, never ourselves, and we only claim what the evidence will actually carry.

The skin microbiome · How we handle evidence

Ethics

Every ingredient is on the label, in plain English, listed most abundant first, with its exact percentage published. That is unusual in a category that treats formulas as trade secrets, and it is deliberate. It sits alongside recyclable aluminium packaging, a purposely small range where each product has to earn its place, and a business being built toward B Corp certification.

Everything on the label · Our ethics

Start wherever you like

Each of these goes a layer deeper. None of them will oversell.

  • The skin microbiome: what it is, why it matters, and what the research is still working out.
  • How we formulate: the three kinds of ingredient that do the real work, and why each one earns its place.
  • How we handle evidence: the line between reviewing science and running it, and what that means for what we will and will not say.
  • Everything on the label: why we publish every ingredient and every percentage, when most of the industry does not.
  • Our ethics: packaging, range, suppliers, and the road to B Corp.

And the proof sits one level down again, in the ingredient library, where each ingredient has its own page and its own references. If you ever want to check our reasoning, that is where to look.

Browse the ingredient library · Find your skin type · Shop the range

nodes.title: The Skin Microbiome
nodes.body:
The bacteria living on your skin are not a problem to be scrubbed away. They are part of how healthy skin works. Here is what the research actually shows, and what it doesn't.

Most of us grow up thinking of bacteria as something to get rid of. Skin tells a more interesting story. Your skin is home to a busy community of bacteria, fungi and other microbes, known collectively as the skin microbiome, and the research suggests they are not passengers. They are part of how skin defends itself and keeps its barrier working. As one review put it, with the microbiome you are never alone.

Why balance matters more than cleanliness

A healthy microbiome tends to be diverse and stable, a bit like a well-planted garden. No single resident takes over, and the mix as a whole keeps things steady.

Some of those residents earn their keep. Beneficial bacteria such as Staphylococcus epidermidis are credited in the research with helping to hold less welcome microbes in check and with supporting the skin barrier. When the community is thrown out of balance, a state researchers call dysbiosis, studies have associated it with conditions including acne, eczema and rosacea.

That association is exactly why balance is worth protecting. It is also where we want to be careful with our words. An association in the research is not a promise that a moisturiser treats any of those conditions, and we would never make that claim. What it does tell us is that skincare has a job to do in not making things worse.

Support, not control

Skin mostly manages its own garden. Often the kindest thing a product can do is avoid trampling it.

Harsh cleansing, high-pH products and heavy fragrance can all disturb the balance, which means a surprising amount of microbiome-friendly formulating is really about what you leave out. We formulate at a skin-friendly, slightly acidic pH, because the research indicates the skin's commensal microbes prefer it, and we leave synthetic fragrance out entirely to lower the risk of irritation. That is the quiet version of microbiome care, and the one best supported by the evidence.

Feeding and steering, gently

Two kinds of ingredient can lend a more active hand, and both work with the microbiome rather than against it.

Prebiotics are food for the microbes already living on your skin. We use inulin, a plant-derived prebiotic. Postbiotics are the useful compounds those microbes produce, and rather than adding live bacteria to a jar, we include a Saccharomyces and barley seed ferment that delivers some of those compounds directly. The research on topical pre- and postbiotics suggests they can help support a balanced microbiome and a calmer barrier.

It is also a young field. A good deal of the microbiome language you will see in skincare runs ahead of the evidence, promising to rebuild or rebalance your skin in ways the studies do not yet support. We would rather say that plainly than join in. So we describe these ingredients as support, and we hold the bolder claims lightly until the science catches up.

What this means for our products

Every Biotaderm moisturiser carries both a prebiotic and a postbiotic, in a gentle base formulated at a skin-friendly pH, with no synthetic fragrance. The aim is modest and deliberate: to work with the system your skin already runs, rather than override it. Support, not control, applied to the smallest residents of all.

How we formulate · Find your skin type · Shop the range

References

  • Grice, E. A., and Segre, J. A. (2011). The skin microbiome. Nature Reviews Microbiology, 9(4), 244-253.
  • Byrd, A. L., Belkaid, Y., and Segre, J. A. (2018). The human skin microbiome. Nature Reviews Microbiology, 16(3), 143-155.
  • Sanford, J. A., and Gallo, R. L. (2013). Functions of the skin microbiota in health and disease. Seminars in Immunology, 25(5), 370-377.
  • Flowers, L., and Grice, E. A. (2020). The skin microbiota: balancing risk and reward. Cell Host and Microbe, 28(2), 190-200.
  • Dréno, B., and others (2016). Microbiome in healthy skin, update for dermatologists. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology, 30(12), 2038-2047.
  • Sfriso, R., and others (2020). Revealing the secret life of skin, with the microbiome you are never alone. International Journal of Cosmetic Science, 42(2), 116-126.
  • Fournière, M., and others (2020). Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes: two major sentinels of skin microbiota and the influence of cosmetics. Microorganisms, 8(11), 1752.
  • Uberoi, A., and others (2021). Commensal microbiota regulates skin barrier function and repair via signalling through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor. Cell Host and Microbe, 29(8), 1235-1248.

nodes.title: How We Formulate
nodes.body:
The thinking behind what goes in, and what stays out.

Every ingredient in a Biotaderm product has to earn its place. If it does not do a job the published evidence supports, it does not go in. If a claim cannot be supported by that evidence, it does not go on the label. That single rule keeps the formulas short, the range small, and the copy honest, and it is why you will not find a long list of on-trend extracts here doing very little.

What you will find is a small number of ingredient types chosen to work together, in a base built to be gentle. The idea running through all of it is the same one that runs through the rest of the brand. Support, not control.

Three kinds of ingredient do the real work

Cold-pressed organic plant oils

The base of every product is cold-pressed organic plant oils, and both of those words are deliberate. Cold pressing avoids the heat and solvents of refining, which means it preserves the bioactive compounds that give a plant oil its character: carotenoids, tocopherols, phytosterols and the phenolics that refined oils tend to lose. The research credits these compounds with antioxidant and skin-conditioning qualities, and there is a practical bonus too, since a higher phenolic content also improves the oil's oxidative stability, so the product stays good for longer.

We choose these oils for what is in them, not for what they cost. The particular oils change with the skin type, but the reasoning does not.

Prebiotics and postbiotics

These are the ingredients that speak to the microbiome directly, and they do it gently. Prebiotics are food for the microbes already living on your skin, and we use inulin, a plant-derived prebiotic. Postbiotics are the useful compounds those microbes produce, and rather than putting live cultures in a jar, we include a Saccharomyces and barley seed ferment that carries some of those compounds ready-made.

The research on topical pre- and postbiotics suggests they can help support a balanced microbiome, though it is a young field and we treat it as support rather than a cure. There is more on all of this on the skin microbiome page.

Atlantic algal extracts

One ingredient ties the whole range to where it is made. Bladderwrack, Fucus vesiculosus, is the same Atlantic seaweed you can see on the rocks along the north Devon coast at low tide. Ours is produced by specialist extractors in France who work with this species properly, so the connection to the coast is one of kinship and origin, not a supply chain we are pretending to have. Its compounds, including phlorotannins, fucoidans and phenolics, are credited in published research with antioxidant activity, and that is the part we lean on.

What we leave out

Good formulation is as much about restraint as addition. We leave out synthetic fragrance entirely, and we never hide anything behind a "parfum" or "fragrance" catch-all. We also leave out fragrance-only ingredients, since these are among the more common triggers for irritation and allergy, and that matters most for sensitive skin. Every ingredient we do use is listed individually, most abundant first, so nothing is ever tucked out of sight.

The one essential oil

There is a single essential oil in the range, and we would rather name it than let you wonder. Vetiver root oil, from Vetiveria Zizanioides, is a natural essential oil obtained from the roots of the grass. It is not a synthetic fragrance and nothing like one. We include it at a low, carefully controlled level, chosen for the antioxidant properties the research credits it with and for the quiet natural note it lends the blend.

It is also unusual in a genuinely useful way. Most essential oils contain at least one of the fragrance allergens that labelling rules require you to declare. Vetiver is one of the few that contains none of them, so there is nothing on that list to declare here. That is a labelling fact, and we keep it separate from the question of comfort, because a concentrated aromatic can still be a lot for a fragile barrier. So the level is kept low, raised only gently across the lighter to richer textures, and if your skin runs reactive it is worth a patch test first.

This is why the honest description of the range is "no synthetic fragrance" rather than "fragrance-free". One is true. The other would not be.

The base, and everything else

Around those actives sits a supporting cast that does the quiet structural work: an olive-derived emulsifier system, plant-derived squalane, a gentle gluconolactone, glycerin, vitamin E and a few others. None of it is hidden. Every ingredient and its exact percentage is published on the product page, and each one has its own entry in the ingredient library if you want the detail and the sources.

Everything on the label · Browse the ingredient library · Find your skin type

nodes.title: How We Handle Evidence
nodes.body:
We read the science. We don't run it. That one line governs everything we say.

Skincare has a trust problem, and most of it comes down to language. Brands borrow the authority of research without doing any, and the reader is left unable to tell a real finding from a well-dressed guess. We would rather be the brand you can check. So it is worth setting out, plainly, how we decide what we are willing to tell you.

We read the science. We don't run it.

Biotaderm reviews published research and formulates on the basis of what it shows. We have not run our own clinical trials, and our copy never implies we have. That distinction sounds small. It is the whole foundation of the trust we are asking for.

So we credit the evidence, not ourselves. When the research supports something, we say the research supports it. We do not quietly promote ourselves to the role of the people who discovered it.

Why the wording matters

You will notice the same phrases throughout the site. The research suggests. Studies indicate. The evidence points to. Those openings are not hedging for its own sake. They are accurate, because they put the credit where it belongs.

The moment a sentence hands Biotaderm the discovery, with an "our research shows" or a "we've proven", it stops being true, and truth is the entire proposition. Here is the test we apply to our own copy. "Our research shows bladderwrack protects the skin" becomes "the research on bladderwrack points to antioxidant activity." Same ingredient, same story, told in a way we can actually stand behind.

What we will, and will not, claim

We make cosmetic claims, not medical ones. A moisturiser can support and comfort skin. It does not treat, cure or reverse anything, and you will not catch us implying otherwise.

We only put a claim on a page when the published evidence supports it. When the evidence is genuinely strong, we will tell you. When it is early, thin, or still being argued over, we will tell you that too, rather than rounding it up into something firmer. A surprising amount of the science we find sits in that honest middle, and pretending otherwise would be the easiest way to lose the very thing this page exists to protect.

Behind every claim

There is more work behind this than the finished copy shows. Before a claim goes on a page, it is weighed against the published literature, and if it is not well enough supported, it does not run. We would rather say less and mean all of it than say more and defend little of it. You do not need to see that process to benefit from it. You just need to know it happens, and that it is deliberately strict.

Honesty is the strategy, not just the ethics

Being accurate where the rest of the category is vague is not only the right thing to do. It is the most durable advantage a small brand can have. It is also why the detail lives out in the open: every ingredient has its own page, with its own references, so you never have to take our word for it. If our reasoning does not hold up, you will be able to see that for yourself.

Browse the ingredient library · The skin microbiome · Everything on the label

nodes.title: Everything on the Label
nodes.body:
Every ingredient, every percentage, published. Here is why we do it, and how to read it.

Most skincare labels tell you what is in a product. Very few tell you how much. That gap is where a lot of the industry's tricks live, and closing it is one of the plainest promises we make. On every Biotaderm product you get the complete formulation: each ingredient, its proper name, and its exact percentage. Nothing rounded away, nothing left to trust.

What we publish

For every product, the full picture is on the page. Each ingredient appears under its INCI name, the standardised name used on labels the world over, with a plain-English name alongside so you are not left translating Latin. The list runs in order of weight, most abundant first, and we carry that order all the way down to the smallest trace, which goes further than the labelling rules actually require. Beside each one sits its exact percentage.

We also mark how ingredients are made. A star means the ingredient is cold-pressed and organic. A caret means it is organic. And where there is an aromatic in the formula, it is named outright as vetiver, never folded into a vague "parfum" or "fragrance". If it is in the bottle, it is on the label, under its own name.

Why percentages, not just a list

A list of ingredients tells you what is present. A percentage tells you whether it is actually doing anything.

This is the quiet test that most transparency stops short of. It is easy to put a fashionable ingredient on a label at a level so low it could not possibly matter, purely so the name can appear on the front of the pack. Publishing the number makes that impossible to hide. If we name an oil as one of the reasons to buy a product, you can see exactly how much of it is in there, and hold us to it. The discipline runs both ways. Knowing the figure will be printed keeps us honest while we are still formulating.

What it lets you do

Transparency is not decoration here. It is meant to be used.

If you react to a particular ingredient, you can check for it before you buy, and see how much is present. If you want to know how rich or how light a formula really is, the numbers tell you rather than the marketing. And if you ever want to compare us honestly against something else, you have the full picture to do it with. We would rather hand you the means to make your own decision than ask you to defer to ours. Skincare that respects your intelligence works better when you can see the workings.

How to read a Biotaderm formulation

It is simpler than it looks. The order is the key: ingredients are listed from most to least, so whatever sits near the top makes up the bulk of the product, and the actives you have read about usually sit lower down, where a little does a lot. Each line gives you the INCI name, the everyday name in brackets, and the percentage. A star after a name means cold-pressed and organic, a caret means organic, and the short legend at the foot of every list spells that out. That is the whole code.

Nothing to hide, by design

Publishing everything is not a marketing flourish we can withdraw when it stops being convenient. It is structural. It is also, as it turns out, our most persuasive argument, because a formula you can inspect in full is a far stronger claim than any adjective. The reasoning behind each ingredient, with its references, sits in the ingredient library, and the discipline behind every claim is set out in how we handle evidence.

Browse the ingredient library · How we handle evidence · Shop the range

nodes.title: Our Ethics
nodes.body:
The standards behind the business, stated plainly and kept to what we can actually stand behind.

Ethics is easy to talk about and harder to prove, which is why so much of it in this industry arrives as warm words and vague badges. We would rather say less and mean it. What follows is what we do, described precisely enough that you could hold us to it, and nothing we cannot yet back up gets dressed up as though we can.

Working toward B Corp

We are building the business toward B Corp certification. That is a company-level standard, not a product one, in which an independent body verifies a company's social and environmental performance, its transparency and its accountability across the whole operation. It is deliberately hard to earn, which is rather the point.

We are in that process, not at the end of it. So we will tell you we are working toward it, and we will only call ourselves certified on the day we actually are. If you ever see us claim otherwise, hold us to this paragraph.

Packaging

We prioritise aluminium. It can be recycled again and again without losing quality, and recycling it takes a fraction of the energy needed to make it new, which is not true of most alternatives. Around that, we keep plastic to a minimum rather than claiming to have none, because honest beats absolute. The aim is packaging that does its job protecting the product and then has somewhere sensible to go afterwards.

A deliberately small range

It would be easy to grow the range for the sake of it. New launches sell, whether or not they add anything. We have chosen the opposite discipline. The range is three textures across five skin types, and each one has to earn its place by doing a real job for a real kind of skin. If a product would only be there to widen the shelf, we do not make it.

Vegan, and cruelty-free

Our products are vegan. They contain no animal-derived ingredients. That is a plain fact, so we state it plainly rather than decorating it.

On cruelty-free, a little honesty is in order. Testing cosmetics on animals is already banned by law in the UK and the EU, so no responsible brand here should be testing on animals in the first place. We treat that as the floor, not as something to award ourselves a medal for. The only person our products get tested on is the chemist who makes them.

The suppliers we choose

We choose suppliers and distributors for their standards, not only their price. That shapes real decisions, from where an ingredient comes from to who we are willing to sell through. We would rather be careful about this than sweeping, so we will not claim to have audited every link in every chain. What we can say is that ethical standing is part of the decision, every time, and not an afterthought.

And what we say

Transparency belongs on this page too, because how a brand talks is an ethical choice as much as a marketing one. We publish every ingredient and every percentage, and we only make claims the published evidence supports. Those are set out in full on everything on the label and how we handle evidence.

The more personal side of why the brand exists lives on the about page. This page is simply the practice behind the principles.

Everything on the label · How we handle evidence · Shop the range

nodes.title: Frequently asked questions
nodes.body:
Everything below is the answer we would give you if you rang. If your question is not here, email us or ring 01288 272800. It reaches Richard, who formulates the products.

Choosing

How do I know which skin type I am?

The skin type finder asks two questions about how your skin actually behaves and points you at one of five types. It takes a couple of minutes.

If you would rather work it out yourself, the short version is this. Skin that feels tight and flakes is dry. Skin that shines by mid-afternoon is oily. Skin that stings or reddens easily is sensitive on top of whichever of those it is. Balanced is the one that mostly behaves itself.

What is the difference between Flow, Core and Deep?

How much cold-pressed oil each one carries. That is the only thing that changes.

Flow is over 9% plant oils, sinks in quickly and is made for the face. Core is over 14%, richer and more cushioning, made for the body. Deep is over 19%, the substantial one for hands, elbows, knees and feet.

Same five oils, same prebiotics and postbiotics, three weights. You are choosing by where you are putting it and how rich you like it to feel.

My face and my body are not the same. Do I need two?

Plenty of people buy two. Face and body genuinely behave differently, and running Flow on the face and Core on the body is a common pairing. Nothing in the range conflicts, so mixing is fine.

If you are starting with one, buy for your face. It is the skin you will notice first.

Is it suitable for sensitive skin?

Two of the five types are built for it, Dry Sensitive and Oily Sensitive, and they are the most careful formulations we make. There is no synthetic fragrance anywhere in the range.

We publish every ingredient and every percentage on every product page, so if there is something your skin has fallen out with before, you can check for it before you buy rather than after.

Using it

How do I use it?

Warm a small amount between your fingertips and press it into clean skin, morning or night or both, before any make-up or sunscreen. On the body, massage it in until it disappears.

Small amount is the operative phrase. These are concentrated, and most people use twice what they need for the first week.

How long before I notice anything?

Surface comfort arrives quickly, often within a few days. Anything to do with the skin barrier takes longer, because skin turns over roughly every four weeks and you are waiting on new cells rather than treating the ones already there.

Give it a fortnight before you judge it. That is why the trial runs for two weeks.

Can I use it under sunscreen or make-up?

Yes. Flow in particular is formulated to sit under both. Give it a minute to absorb and everything else goes on more evenly.

Should I patch test first?

If your skin reacts easily, yes. A small amount on the inner forearm, left for 24 hours, tells you most of what you need to know. If your skin is generally uneventful, you can skip it.

How long does a bottle last, and how long does it keep once opened?

A 150ml bottle used twice a day on the face lasts most people around three months. On the body it goes faster, because there is more of you.

Once opened, use it within six months. That is the small open-jar symbol on the bottle with 6M beside it. The batch number and date are on the base.

What is in it

Why do you publish the whole formulation?

Because you can read it. Every product page carries every ingredient and its exact percentage, in a table, each one linked to a page explaining what it is doing and what the evidence behind it says.

An ingredient list tells you what is in a product. The percentage tells you whether it is doing a job or decorating the label.

Does it have a scent?

A faint earthy one, from a single ingredient. Vetiver root oil, a natural essential oil taken from the roots of a grass, at between 0.10% and 0.20% depending on the texture.

There is no synthetic fragrance in the range, and no "parfum" catch-all standing in for a list of components we have not named. A concentrated aromatic can still be a lot for a fragile barrier, so we keep the level low and say plainly that it is there.

What keeps it from going off?

Sodium benzoate at 0.38%, working with gluconolactone and the pH that the sodium citrate holds. It is a preservative system used widely across food and cosmetics, and it is on the label like everything else.

A water-based cream with nothing preserving it grows things within days. That is chemistry rather than opinion.

Is it vegan, and is it tested on animals?

Every ingredient is plant, mineral or ferment derived, so the range suits a vegan routine. Nothing is tested on animals. Testing cosmetics on animals has been illegal in the UK since 1998.

We hold no certification for either at the moment.

Is it organic?

Many of the oils are, and they are marked on every formulation table. An asterisk means cold-pressed and organic. A caret means organic.

The finished products are not certified organic. Certification covers the whole product and the whole process, and we have not been through it.

What is all the microbiome talk about?

Your skin carries its own community of bacteria and fungi. The research points fairly consistently in one direction: skin tends to do better when that community is supported rather than stripped.

So three things in every formula are aimed at it. Inulin, a prebiotic that feeds the microbes already living there. A Saccharomyces and barley seed ferment, which is a postbiotic. And chlorella. There is no synthetic fragrance and no harsh surfactant working against them.

The caveat belongs here too. Skin microbiome science is young, and a good deal of it is still in cell culture rather than on faces. Our Science sets out what the evidence supports and where it runs out.

Buying

What if it does not suit me?

Give it two weeks. If it is still not right, we will swap it for a different skin type or refund you, whichever you prefer, any time up to 60 days after your order arrives. Return postage is on us, and you send back whatever is left in the bottle.

Sometimes we will simply refund you and tell you to keep it. One claim per product, per customer, and the full terms are in the refund policy.

What does delivery cost, and how quickly will it arrive?

Standard delivery is £5.99, and free on orders over £40. Express is £7.99, free over £80. If you are in one of nine north Devon postcodes, orders over £20 come free and we bring them to you ourselves.

Everything is made by hand in small batches. If what you have ordered is in stock we dispatch within one to two working days. If it is not, we make it for you and dispatch within seven days. We deliver across the UK and nowhere else for now.

What is the refill bottle, and why is it only a pound less?

The refill is the same 150ml aluminium bottle with the same cream in it, and no pump. The pump is the only plastic part. It is designed to move from bottle to bottle and it lasts for years.

A pound is roughly what the pump costs us, so the saving is the pump coming off the price rather than a reward for buying less.

If this is your first order, buy the version with the pump. A refill on its own is a bottle you cannot easily get the cream out of.

Why aluminium?

Because it recycles indefinitely without losing quality, which is not true of plastic. The bottle is refillable and the pump is meant to be reused. That combination does more than a recycling symbol on a plastic bottle ever will.

Do you sell anywhere other than online?

Not yet. We are talking to a handful of independent shops in north Devon. If you run one and would like to stock us, email us.

nodes.title: Cookie Policy
nodes.body:
Last updated 11 August 2026.

What cookies are

A cookie is a small text file a website puts on your device so it can remember something. Some are essential. Most are not, and those need your permission before they run.

This policy covers cookies and the technologies that work like them, including pixels, tags and local storage. We refer to all of them as cookies here.

Welcombe Skincare Ltd, trading as Biotaderm, is responsible for the cookies described below. We are registered in England and Wales under company number 13451607 at Darracott Farm, Welcombe, Devon EX39 6HG, and registered with the Information Commissioner's Office under reference ZB377476.

Your choice

When you first visit biotaderm.com you are asked whether to accept cookies that are not strictly necessary. You can accept all, reject all, or choose by category. Rejecting is exactly as easy as accepting, and rejecting does not stop you shopping.

You can change your mind whenever you like using the Cookie settings link in the footer. Your choice is remembered for six months, after which we ask again.

You can also block or delete cookies in your browser settings. Blocking strictly necessary cookies will stop the basket and checkout working.

The three kinds we use

Strictly necessary. These make the shop function: keeping items in your basket, keeping you signed in, getting you through checkout securely, and remembering your cookie choice. They do not need your consent, because the site cannot work without them.

Analytics. These tell us how many people visit, which pages they read and where they leave, so we can make the site better. They run only if you accept them.

Advertising. These let us measure whether our advertising works, and let us send you a reminder if you leave something in your basket. They run only if you accept them.

Some of these companies are based outside the UK. Where information moves abroad, the transfer is covered by a UK adequacy decision or by approved safeguards such as the UK International Data Transfer Agreement, so it keeps the protection it has here.

What happens if you say no

The shop works exactly as it does otherwise. You can browse, order and check out. We simply see less about how the site is used, and our advertising is measured less precisely. That is our problem rather than yours.

Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control

If your browser sends a Global Privacy Control signal, we treat it as a refusal of analytics and advertising cookies and honour it automatically.
